prompt: A dashboard using the empirical nearest-rank convention says the 99th-percentile (p99) latency is 420 ms. Which interpretation is correct, allowing ties?

options.explanation: Percentiles are about fractions of all requests, not a count of 99.

options.text: The average latency of the slowest 1% is 420 ms
options.explanation: That would be a tail conditional mean, not a percentile threshold; a trimmed mean conventionally discards tail observations.

options.text: At least 99% of recorded requests took 420 ms or less; no more than 1% were slower
options.explanation: Correct for nearest rank. Ties and finite sample ranks can make the fraction at or below the threshold greater than 99%.
A percentile describes the spread of the data, not the uncertainty of an estimate.

workedExample:
The nearest-rank p99 is read off at this position in the sorted list:

```formula
r = ⌈0.99 × n⌉
where
r: the rank (position, counting from the smallest) of the reported value
n: the number of observations
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round up to the next whole number
0.99: 99%, the percentile as a fraction
In words: go 99% of the way along the sorted latencies, rounding up, and report the value there.
```

At least r observations are at or below it; ties can put still more there. The percentile says nothing about how slow the remaining observations are.

prompt: A search page fans out to 100 backend shards and must wait for all of them. Each shard independently exceeds its own 99th-percentile latency 1% of the time. What fraction of page loads see at least one slow shard?

options.explanation: Correct. 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.634. A per-shard tail event becomes the common case for users.
Each shard is slow 1% of the time, but the page waits on 100 of them. The chance at least one is slow is much higher.
100 × 1% = 100% is the union bound, which overestimates. Sometimes all 100 shards are fast (about 37% of the time).
Scaling a probability by the square root of the call count is not the rule for a union. Use the complement of all 100 calls being fast.

workedExample:
```formula
P(F) = 0.99^100 ≈ 0.366
P(¬F) = 1 − 0.366 ≈ 0.634
where
F: the event "all 100 shards are fast"
¬F: "not F", at least one shard is slow
0.99: the chance one shard is fast
0.99^100: 100 copies of 0.99 multiplied together, using independence
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
≈: approximately equal to
In words: all 100 shards are fast only about 37% of the time, so about 63% of page loads wait on a slow shard.
```

This is the central argument of *The Tail at Scale*: in fan-out systems, user latency is governed by backend tail latency. Mitigations include hedged requests (send a backup after a chosen delay; the 95th percentile is one possible policy, subject to extra load and request semantics) and reducing fan-out.

link.title: The Tail at Scale — Dean and Barroso, CACM 2013

prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import math

def pct(xs, p):
    s = sorted(xs)
    # Convert percentile to sorted rank.
    k = math.ceil(p / 100 * len(s))
    return s[max(k - 1, 0)]

lat = [12, 15, 11, 240, 14,
       13, 16, 12, 900, 14]
print(pct(lat, 90))
```

options.explanation: 900 is the maximum, i.e. the 100th percentile. The nearest-rank 90th percentile of 10 values is the 9th smallest.
16 is the 8th smallest value. Rounding 0.9 × 10 = 9 up gives 9, so the 9th is chosen.
Correct. The sorted observations are 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 240 and 900. The requested rank is nine, so the code returns the element at Python index eight: 240.
128 might come from averaging 16 and 240. Nearest rank returns an actual observation, without interpolation.

workedExample:
1. Sort: `[11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 240, 900]`.
2. Find the rank:

```formula
k = ⌈90 / 100 × 10⌉ = ⌈9.0⌉ = 9
where
k: the rank to read (the variable k in the code)
90: the percentile asked for (p in the code)
10: the number of values, len(s)
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round up to a whole number (math.ceil in the code)
In words: the 90th percentile of 10 values is the 9th smallest.
```

3. Python lists count from 0, so index k − 1 = 8 gives 240.

Note how two outliers dominate: the 50th percentile is 14 ms, the 90th is 240 ms. With only 10 samples, these tail estimates are very noisy.

prompt: You run 4 API servers. Each reports its own 99th-percentile (p99) latency every minute. Which approaches give a fleet-wide p99 calculation or an explicitly approximate estimate from combined data over the same time window? Select all that apply.

options.text: Average the four servers' p99 values
options.explanation: Percentiles don't average. If one server handles most traffic or has a very different distribution, the mean of p99s can be far from the true fleet p99.

options.text: Have each server export a latency histogram with shared bucket boundaries, sum the histograms, and compute p99 from the merged histogram
options.explanation: Correct. Histograms with the same buckets merge by adding counts, and the percentile is then computed from the combined distribution (to bucket precision).

options.text: Take the maximum of the four p99 values
options.explanation: Under nearest rank, the maximum is an upper bound on the fleet p99, but need not equal it and can be badly wrong when traffic is uneven.

options.text: Send every raw latency to a central store and compute p99 over all of them
options.explanation: Correct, if expensive: with all observations, you can compute the exact percentile.

options.text: Use compatible t-digest sketches or compatible HdrHistogram histograms, and merge them over the same time window
options.explanation: Correct. Both representations support merging compatible summaries of the observations. Their quantiles are estimates with representation error; they do not arise by averaging individual percentile values.

workedExample:
Percentiles are not linear: the p99 of two servers' combined requests is not a function of the two servers' p99 values alone.

Counterexample: server A has 1,000 requests all at 10 ms (p99 of 10 milliseconds). Server B has 10 requests all at 1,000 ms (p99 of 1,000 milliseconds). Combined, 10 of 1,010 requests (about 1%) are slow, so the nearest-rank fleet p99 is 10 ms, not the average 505 ms or the max 1,000 ms.

```formula
r = ⌈0.99 × 1010⌉ = ⌈999.9⌉ = 1000
where
r: the nearest-rank position of the fleet p99 in the sorted combined list
1010: the total number of requests, 1,000 + 10
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round up to a whole number
In words: the fleet p99 is the 1,000th fastest of 1,010 requests, which is still one of server A's 10 ms requests.
```

Correct approaches keep enough of each distribution to combine: raw data, histograms with shared buckets (Prometheus), or mergeable sketches.
